prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, Senate, The

outputs.L1:
All we know of history  
we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone  
on the Senate floor:

The Flood makes graves of the fields,  
and the angels harvest enough suffering  
to live for another thousand years.

Moses pulls off his beard and lights a cigarette:  
“I’m tired of pretending.”

He pushes his box of spare commandments under his bed,  
and as he drifts to sleep, his eyes, like caves,  
fill with paintings of woolly rhinos.

Sailing ships forest a small island.  
One light shines from a caravel — the captain’s quarters.  
It’s Christopher Columbus.

All night, he’s been sewing shrouds  
as arrival gifts for the natives.  
Little Chris presses his bleeding fingers to his mouth  
and cries quietly, “No one appreciates me.”

God and the devil tuck him into bed.  
“It’ll get better,” they say.

Together, they complete the shrouds for him,  
while he dreams of golden nipples.

As it was, it is now.

Spring translates the earth into hope —  
tongues of grass taste the sea salt on the west wind  
and the blood on soldiers’ boots.

This morning, one of the old poets —  
unkillable cockroach — cycled past me, yelling,  
“You have the brightest light in America! Ha ha!”

On my dresser, a spider makes a web  
along the contours of my bra.

We lie on the bed together;  
I run my hand up the muscles of your leg  
and feel its eons of evolution,  
now outlawed by the Senate.
outputs.L2:
Everything history gives us  
comes through fragments set in bone,  
a mosaic spread across the Senate floor:

The Flood turns open land into burial ground,  
and angels gather such an abundance of pain  
they can survive on it for the next millennium.

Moses tears away his beard, strikes a match,  
and smokes, saying,  
I’m done acting.

He slides his crate of extra commandments beneath the bed,  
and while sleep takes him, his cave-dark eyes  
crowd with images of woolly rhinoceroses painted on stone.

A cluster of sailing vessels crowds around a little island.  
From one caravel, a single lamp burns —  
the captain’s room.

There sits Christopher Columbus.

He has spent the whole night stitching funeral cloths  
to present to the people waiting onshore.

Small Chris puts his cut fingers against his lips  
and weeps softly:  
Nobody values what I do.

God and Satan pull the covers over him.  
Things will improve, they tell him.

Side by side, they finish sewing the shrouds in his place,  
while he sleeps and imagines nipples made of gold.

What happened before continues happening.

Spring renders the world as possibility —  
blades of grass, like tongues, sample the ocean brine  
carried inland by the western wind,  
and also the blood dried on soldiers’ shoes.

This morning, an elderly poet —  
a cockroach too stubborn to die —  
rode by me on a bicycle, shouting,  
You have the strongest radiance in America! Ha ha!

On my dresser, a spider spins silk  
following the shape of my bra.

We stretch out on the bed beside one another;  
my palm travels along the strength of your leg,  
and I sense the deep ages of its making,  
the long evolution  
the Senate has now forbidden.
outputs.L3:
The text presents history as a broken and violent record rather than as a coherent story of progress. The past appears fragmented, filled with suffering, myth, conquest, and political domination. Instead of offering clear moral lessons or heroic narratives, history is shown as chaotic and brutal, shaped by those who hold power and by the pain of those who are subjected to it.

Religious and historical figures are reimagined in unsettling and often absurd ways. They are not treated as noble, distant, or untouchable icons, but as weary, flawed, and morally compromised figures. This treatment strips away grandeur and exposes the contradictions behind traditional accounts of faith, empire, and civilization. By making these figures seem ridiculous or exhausted, the poem questions the authority of the stories that have been passed down through religion and history.

Columbus, in particular, is depicted not as a heroic explorer but as a figure associated with death, exploitation, and destruction. His arrival brings violence and suffering rather than discovery or enlightenment. Yet he is also shown seeking pity and validation, as though he wants sympathy despite the devastation he represents. This creates a bitter irony: the agent of conquest appears to ask for emotional recognition while ignoring the suffering caused by his actions.

The poem also connects historical violence to the present. It suggests that oppression is not confined to the past but continues in new forms. The brutality of conquest, political control, and social domination remains active, even if it appears under different names or systems. In this way, the poem refuses to treat history as something safely finished. Instead, it presents the past as something that still shapes contemporary fear, injustice, and violence.

Alongside these political and historical concerns, the poem includes moments of personal intimacy and natural renewal. Bodies, reproduction, and evolution appear as signs of life and continuity, but they are also surrounded by anxiety and control. The natural processes of growth and change are placed beside political fear, suggesting that even the most private or biological aspects of life are affected by systems of power. The poem therefore moves between the intimate and the historical, showing how personal life cannot be separated from larger forces of violence, authority, and survival.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a dense and unsettling meditation on history, religion, conquest, and political domination. Rather than treating these subjects as separate or distant from one another, it fuses them into a single symbolic landscape. Biblical scenes, the figure of Columbus, images of war, natural elements, and intimate bodily experiences appear together in surreal and anachronistic combinations. This collapse of time makes the past feel urgently present: religious myth, colonial violence, and modern systems of control are shown as part of the same continuing structure.

Through its strange and fragmented imagery, the poem suggests that history is not a linear sequence of completed events. Instead, the violences of conquest, empire, and oppression repeat across different eras under new names and forms. Columbus becomes more than a historical figure; he stands for invasion, possession, and the rewriting of memory by those in power. Biblical references similarly become charged with political meaning, as sacred narratives are placed beside scenes of suffering, coercion, and destruction. The result is a world in which religion, history, and political authority are all implicated in acts of domination.

The poem also connects large-scale historical brutality to the private and physical experience of the body. The body is not protected from history; it becomes one of the places where history is felt, recorded, and violated. Images of flesh, sensation, and vulnerability make political violence intimate rather than abstract. The speaker’s present moment cannot be separated from the accumulated force of earlier atrocities, because those atrocities continue to shape identity, memory, and lived experience.

In this way, the poem resists any attempt to erase or sanitize the past. It exposes how systems of power depend on forgetting, distortion, and enforced silence. By bringing together incompatible times and images, the poem creates a symbolic mosaic that reveals hidden continuities between biblical violence, colonial conquest, warfare, and contemporary political control. Its vision is bleak but purposeful: it insists that the past remains active in the present, and that personal existence is inseparable from the historical and political forces that have shaped it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem that blends biblical imagery, Columbus, American politics, evolution, erotic intimacy, and dark humor, in a contemporary apocalyptic voice.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Maps Catch Fire**

In the beginning  
there was a press conference,  
and the void had good lighting.

God leaned over the lectern  
with a mouth full of thunder  
and said, Let there be—

but the microphones cut out,  
and somewhere in the feedback  
a lobbyist invented night.

Columbus was there, naturally,  
still lost, still confident,  
dragging his little wooden apocalypse  
across the wet blue animal of the world.

He planted a flag  
in the ribcage of morning  
and called it discovery.

The angels took notes.  
The devils filed paperwork.  
The natives looked at the horizon  
and saw history approaching  
in a hat.

O America,  
you magnificent vending machine  
full of bullets and psalms,

your senators rise like damp bread,  
your presidents wear the faces  
of emergency exits,

your prophets sell freeze-dried salvation  
between ads for gold,  
mattresses,  
and pills that promise the dead  
will want us again.

On the seventh day  
God rested  
because the polling was inconclusive.

By then the oceans had learned  
to climb stairs.

By then the forests  
were coughing up receipts.

By then the children  
were drawing dinosaurs  
with human faces  
and asking if extinction  
comes with a tracking number.

Darwin, old tender undertaker,  
stood knee-deep in the Galápagos  
holding a finch like a question.

Behold, he said,  
the beak changes.

Behold, said the serpent,  
so does the appetite.

And we evolved  
from mud to mammal,  
from mammal to market,  
from market to meme,  
dragging our holy thumbs  
over glass rectangles  
while the moon turned yellow  
as an old tooth.

Still, beloved,  
you came to me  
in the hour of sirens,

your hair smelling faintly  
of rain and catastrophe,  
your hands unbuttoning the evening  
from my spine.

We made a small republic  
beneath the blanket,

no flags,  
no founding fathers,  
only the warm impeachment  
of loneliness,

only your breath voting yes  
against my throat,

only the ancient campaign  
of skin for skin  
while outside  
the horsemen circled the block  
looking for parking.

Death arrived first  
in a sensible car.

War had a podcast.

Famine was gluten-free.

Pestilence kept refreshing  
the dashboard numbers  
and saying, Actually,  
if you look at the curve—

We laughed  
because laughter is the last candle  
in the bunker,

because the skull grins  
even when it has no joke,

because Jonah was swallowed  
by the whale  
and still had the nerve  
to complain about the accommodations.

Above us,  
satellites blinked like cherubim  
with security clearance.

Below us,  
the dead practiced democracy  
by raising their hands  
all at once.

Moses came down from the mountain  
with two tablets,  
but one needed charging  
and the other  
had updated its terms of service.

He smashed them anyway.

The golden calf  
was now a golden algorithm  
chewing through the desert,  
predicting our thirst  
before we felt it.

And Columbus, still sailing,  
hit the edge of the map  
and fell upward,

past burning precincts,  
past evangelical billboards,  
past the revolving door  
of heaven,

crying Land! Land!  
at every cloud.

But there is no new world,  
only the old one  
wearing another wound.

Only the ark  
with no insurance.

Only the dove  
returning with a plastic olive branch  
and a tiny lawsuit  
in its beak.

Beloved,  
if the stars go out tonight,  
let them find us unashamed,

two animals  
lit by the last blue weather  
of the television,

evolution’s awkward miracle  
tangled in the sheets,

laughing softly  
while the trumpets practice,

while the sea recites our names  
to the shore,

while God,  
poor God,  
searches His pockets  
for the receipt.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the style of a provocative modern American poet, with historical and religious figures behaving mundanely, violent colonial imagery, and a final turn toward the body and the Senate.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in the exact style of a living modern poet, but here’s an original prose poem using a provocative contemporary mode, with the elements you requested:

The saints were in the laundromat, feeding quarters to the machines with the grave tenderness of men who had once been painted with gold around their heads. Joan of Arc folded gym socks. Moses complained about the price of detergent. Jefferson, immaculate in a white shirt, kept checking the dryers as if land might still be tumbling inside them, warm and stolen. Outside, the old ships came again—not as ships but as receipts, school names, sugar in the coffee, a road cut straight through the burial ground. Horses screamed in the textbooks. A governor smiled with his hand on a map, and the map bled obediently into rivers. Someone was always discovering a country already full of people. Someone was always blessing the blade before supper.

At the diner, Mary ordered eggs over easy and did not look up when the angels entered wearing reflective vests. Christ took a number at the DMV. Buddha held the door for a woman carrying a plastic bag of oranges. The conquistador at the counter asked for more napkins. No one stabbed him. That was the problem. History sat there chewing ice, its mouth red, its boots under the table. The waitress called everyone honey because the empire had made language cheap and sticky, because mercy could still be poured from a dented pot if you tipped it hard enough.

By evening the sky had the color of a bruise pressed under glass. I walked home past statues trying to remember their victims’ names and flags snapping like dogs at the courthouse. My body, meanwhile, kept making its small arguments: hunger, pulse, the wet parliament of the lungs. I put my hand beneath my shirt and felt the nation there, not as anthem but as organ, not as law but as heat. Somewhere the Senate was still in session, robed in its ancient skin, debating whether the wound was a wound or only another opening through which to speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem beginning with “All we know of history” and moving through Moses, Noah’s Flood, Christopher Columbus, God and the devil, spring, war, and a lover’s leg.
counterfactuals.output:
All we know of history  
fits in the wet mouth of a bell—  
bronze remembering fire,  
fire remembering hands,  
hands pretending they never trembled.

Moses comes down the mountain  
with weather in his beard,  
two tablets under each arm  
like doors torn from a house of thunder.  
Below him, the people dance  
around a golden misunderstanding.  
Above him, God is still speaking  
in smoke.

Then water revises the world.

Noah counts the animals by twos,  
but not the ghosts,  
not the drowned lullabies,  
not the chairs floating upside down  
like little wooden prayers.  
The dove returns with a leaf  
and everyone calls it mercy.  
No one asks the leaf.

Centuries later, Columbus  
sails west into an error  
and names it discovery.  
The ocean keeps its face blank.  
The stars do not testify.  
On the shore, history sharpens  
its quill with a knife.

God and the devil sit together  
in a spring orchard,  
sharing one apple,  
arguing over who invented hunger.  
Blossoms fall into their laps  
like tiny white flags.  
The devil says: beauty is evidence.  
God says: evidence of what?

Meanwhile, war pulls on its boots.  
War kisses its children on the forehead.  
War writes home in a language  
made entirely of smoke.  
In the field, the grass rises again,  
green and shameless,  
threading itself through helmets,  
through ribs,  
through the buttons of dead uniforms.

And you—  
you lift your skirt to step over a puddle,  
and your lover’s leg flashes there,  
ordinary, mortal, bright—  
a column of warm weather,  
a road leading out of empire,  
the briefest scripture.

Spring enters without permission.  
It paints the ruins yellow.  
It puts bees in the mouths of cannons.  
It makes the graves look almost  
like they are listening.

All we know of history  
is that it keeps beginning  
with a body,  
a flood,  
a voyage,  
a commandment broken,  
a blossom opening,  
a soldier falling,  
a hand on a thigh  
under the table of the world,

and someone saying:  
remember this,

and someone else  
already forgetting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surrealist political poem about history as a mosaic of violence, featuring biblical scenes, colonial conquest, a spider on lingerie, and evolution being outlawed.
counterfactuals.output:
History is a cathedral built from broken teeth,  
each century a shard pressed into wet mortar,  
gold leaf over the screams, a saint’s face  
assembled from the helmets of the dead.

In Eden, the serpent wears a magistrate’s wig,  
cross-examining the apple.  
Cain invents the border with a jawbone.  
Noah, drunk on the deck, watches the drowned  
rise like ballots from the blackened sea,  
each one stamped with the seal of a king  
not yet born.

Then come the ships—  
white ribs of hunger nosing the horizon,  
their sails swollen with scripture and gunpowder.  
A cross is planted like a knife in the soil.  
The map blooms with fever.  
The conquistador kneels, kisses the crucifix,  
and names the river after his mother  
while the river carries mothers away.

In the governor’s bedroom, a spider  
walks delicately over black lingerie,  
its legs spelling treaties in silk,  
its web a lacework empire—  
small, exquisite machinery  
for catching the soft-bodied future.

Meanwhile the priests of the latest republic  
outlaw evolution:  
no fin may dream of a lung,  
no ape may remember the star,  
no child may draw a ladder  
between mud and angel.  
The fossils are arrested at dawn.  
Darwin is buried again and again  
beneath schoolhouse flags,  
but his worms keep writing in the dark.

O history, mosaic of bayonet, bone, and bread,  
you glitter because you are shattered.  
You hang in the palace vestibule  
where ministers wipe blood from their cuffs  
and call it restoration.  
You hang in the church apse  
where Mary’s blue veil is made  
from the uniforms of occupied boys.  
You hang in the museum, labeled  
Progress, Provenance Unknown.

And still the stones whisper:  
Abel’s blood was not the first river,  
nor was empire the last flood.  
Under every throne, a seed splits its shell.  
Under every decree, a claw becomes a hand.  
Under every forbidden ancestor,  
the forbidden animal keeps climbing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly comic free verse piece where Moses smokes, Columbus sews shrouds for Indigenous people, angels harvest suffering, and the poem ends with intimacy under threat from American politics.
counterfactuals.output:
Moses lights another cigarette  
off the burning bush,  
squints through the sacred smoke  
and says,  

Well, this is awkward.  

The commandments arrive  
already cracked,  
already sponsored,  
already translated  
into a language  
that can acquit a king.

Somewhere west of an old map’s edge,  
Columbus sits cross-legged  
on a deck slick with prayers,  
threading a needle  
with empire’s tiny, shining lie.  

He sews shrouds  
for Indigenous people  
and calls it discovery,  
calls the stitch a coastline,  
calls the blood  
a kind of weather.

Above him, angels in work gloves  
descend with baskets.  
They do not sing.  
They harvest suffering  
by the bushel—  
war grief, border grief,  
hospital grief, grief  
with a child’s shoe still tied.  

They weigh it, stamp it,  
send it upstairs  
where the divine accountants  
laugh so hard  
their halos slip.

Moses coughs.  
The sea refuses to part.  
It has seen enough paperwork.  

Columbus pricks his thumb  
and curses the needle  
for remembering.

And here we are,  
trying to make a room  
inside the sirens,  
your hand under my shirt  
like contraband,  
my mouth at your shoulder  
asking for asylum.

On the television, America  
sharpens its little flags.  
Men with clean cuffs  
argue over which bodies  
belong to the future.

So we turn the volume down,  
not off—  
never off—  
and hold each other  
as if love were illegal already,  

as if the knock  
could come any minute,  

as if the bed itself  
had been gerrymandered  
against us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
